opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to see it is that complex software work is fundamentally a coordination problem, not just a coding problem. A single model, no matter how strong, still faces a context limit and a attention limit. When a project involves many files, many dependencies, and many decisions that have to stay consistent over a long time, you naturally want to split the work. Human engineering organizations already do this: you have someone thinking about architecture, people implementing modules, people writing tests, people reviewing. A multi-agent system is, in some sense, rediscovering that structure.

But I don't think we should simply copy the human org chart. Humans divide labor partly because of communication costs and partly because each person has limited skills. Agents have different constraints. They can be cloned instantly, they can share memory if you design it that way, and they can run in parallel at a scale no team can. So the interesting question is what the right decomposition looks like when the cost of spinning up another "engineer" is close to zero, but the cost of keeping everyone consistent is still high.

In my view there are a few key pieces. First, you need a planner, or orchestrator, that holds the global picture: what is the goal, what are the interfaces, what has been decided. Second, you have workers that go deep on bounded subtasks with a clean, focused context. That's actually one of the biggest benefits: each sub-agent doesn't get polluted by irrelevant history, so it reasons better. Third, and this is often underestimated, you need verification. Tests, execution feedback, reviewers that check the work against the spec. Without a strong verification loop, errors from one agent compound across the system, and multi-agent just becomes multi-mistake.

The harder part is long-horizon consistency. Software is full of implicit contracts. If one agent changes an interface and another agent doesn't know, things break. So the shared state, how agents write down decisions, how they hand off, how conflicts get resolved, matters as much as the model quality itself.

And longer term, I think a lot of this structure will be learned rather than hand-designed. Today we write the orchestration logic manually: this agent does this, that agent does that. But if you train models with reinforcement learning on real end-to-end tasks, the model can learn when to delegate, how to split a problem, and how to merge results. That's similar to what we've seen elsewhere in AI: the hand-crafted pipeline works first, and then a more general, learned approach eventually surpasses it. So multi-agent is less a fixed architecture and more a capability the model itself should grow into, the ability to manage complexity by organizing its own work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses splitting work among agents and says a learned system could eventually learn to split problems and merge results. It does not propose organizing the work as repeated cycles of forking task-specific agents and merging their work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful way to see it is to start from how real software organizations work. A complex project is never one person doing everything in sequence. It's decomposed: someone owns the architecture, someone owns a module, someone writes tests, someone reviews. The reason that works isn't just parallelism, it's that each person holds a bounded context. They know their piece deeply and they don't need the whole system in their head at once.

That's exactly the constraint a model faces. Context is finite, and attention degrades as it fills. So when we think about multi-agent systems for software, the first-order question isn't "how many agents," it's "how do you partition the problem so each agent's context stays clean and relevant." A planner agent that holds the high-level structure and task graph, worker agents that each take a well-specified subtask with just the files and interfaces they need, and then verifier or reviewer agents that look at the result with fresh eyes. The fresh-eyes part matters a lot. A single agent that wrote the code is biased toward believing it works. A separate agent that only sees the spec and the diff catches different things.

The second thing I'd emphasize is that the interface between agents has to be explicit. In human teams, a lot of coordination happens through tacit shared understanding, and that's actually the failure mode we want to avoid. Agents should communicate through artifacts: a task description, a contract for the interface, test cases, a structured report back. If the handoff is a vague natural-language summary, errors compound. If it's a file, a test suite, a concrete acceptance criterion, you get something closer to a build system than to a group chat, and that's much more reliable.

Third, I think the hierarchy should be dynamic rather than fixed. Sometimes a subtask turns out to be much bigger than the planner expected, and the worker should be able to spawn its own sub-decomposition. Sometimes two workers discover they're touching the same interface and need to reconcile. So the structure is less like a fixed org chart and more like a recursive process: any node can become a planner for its own subtree when the problem demands it.

And the last point, which I think people underestimate, is that the system's real leverage comes from the environment, not from agent-to-agent talking. Running the tests, compiling, executing the code, hitting the actual API. Those give ground-truth signal. A lot of what makes long-horizon software work possible is that the agents are constantly checking themselves against reality rather than against each other's opinions. Multi-agent is really a way to scale up how much verified work you can do per unit of context, and verification against the real environment is what makes the whole thing converge instead of drift.

r001.rationale: The response describes assigning subtasks to agents and recursively decomposing work, but it does not clearly propose repeated cycles of forking agents and merging their work.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is how you decompose the work and how the agents coordinate. For a complex software project, you could have one agent clarify the requirements, others implement different components, and another test whether those components work together. But assigning roles is only the beginning. They need a shared understanding of the interfaces, the constraints, and what counts as a successful result.

Some tasks can happen in parallel, while others depend on decisions being settled first. So you need a coordination mechanism that tracks those dependencies and brings problems back to the right agent. If testing reveals a design issue, the system should be able to revise the design rather than just keep patching the implementation.

The important question is whether adding agents actually reduces the effort required to get a correct result. More agents also means more communication and more opportunities for inconsistent assumptions. I would start with a simple structure, give each agent a clear scope, and use tests and integration checkpoints to keep everyone grounded in the same working software.

r001.rationale: The response discusses assigning agents, coordinating dependencies, and integrating components, but it does not propose repeated cycles of forking task-specific agents and merging their work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is how you divide the work and how the agents coordinate. If you simply ask several agents to solve the same problem, you may get more output, but you also create more work checking and combining it.

For complex software work, I would start with a shared understanding of the goal, then assign fairly clear responsibilities. One agent might investigate the codebase, another implement a component, and another review the changes. They need explicit interfaces and a way to share evidence—what they changed, what they tested, and what remains uncertain.

The difficult part is integration. Two changes can each look correct and still fail together. So you need a coordination loop that checks the whole system, revises the plan, and brings decisions back to a human when the requirements are ambiguous. The measure of success should be whether the system delivers reliable software, rather than how many agents are working at once.

r001.rationale: The response describes assigning agents clear responsibilities and coordinating their work through integration cycles, but it does not propose repeatedly forking task-specific agents and merging their work.
